papers.title: Sub-national heterogeneity in the time-varying reproduction number during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: a hierarchical Bayesian analysis
papers.abstract: National-level estimates of the time-varying reproduction number (Rt) for the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BDBV) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have converged on a value close to the epidemic threshold since early August 2026, consistent with independent joint Bayesian renewal-model estimates. A single national Rt, however, can obscure divergent sub-national epidemic trajectories, particularly across a five-province outbreak in which provinces range from a declining original epicentre to recently-seeded fronts. We estimated Rt at national, provincial, and, where case volume allowed, health-zone level, using both a standard sliding-window (Cori) estimator and a hierarchical Bayesian renewal model with partial pooling across spatial units, fitted by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (No-U-Turn Sampler). Provincial estimates diverged materially from the national trend: as of the week of 6 August 2026, Ituri, the outbreak's original epicentre, had a hierarchical median Rt of 0.91 (95% credible interval [CrI] 0.68 - 1.24), while Nord-Kivu (1.23, [0.87 - 1.72]) and Haut-Uele (1.79, [1.24 - 2.67]) remained above threshold. Health-zone disaggregation, feasible only in Ituri and Nord-Kivu given case volume, showed this provincial picture itself masked further heterogeneity: in Ituri, the zone where the outbreak began (Mongbwalu) had clearly declined (Rt 0.36, [0.17 - 0.74]) while the two largest zones by cumulative case count (Bunia, Rwampara) remained at or above threshold; in Nord-Kivu, elevated transmission was concentrated in a single zone (Katwa, Rt 1.39, [0.85 - 1.99]) while a comparably-sized zone (Butembo) had already declined (0.64, [0.23 - 1.38]). An initial disagreement between the sliding-window and hierarchical provincial estimates was traced to a data-reconstruction artefact (forward-filling, rather than interpolating, multi-day gaps in health-zone reporting) rather than a genuine methods disagreement, and resolved once corrected. The hierarchical model's dispersion structure, calibration, and sensitivity to the generation-interval assumption were each checked explicitly; a shared (non-province-specific) dispersion parameter was retained on the basis of negligible predictive difference (PSIS-LOO), the model achieved 95.0% pooled 95% posterior-predictive interval coverage, and the province ranking was unchanged across a generation-interval sensitivity grid (Spearman {rho} = 1.0). Aggregation masks meaningful heterogeneity in transmission intensity at every spatial resolution examined; response prioritisation based on a single national or even provincial Rt risks directing attention away from the specific zones where transmission remains supercritical.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess sub-national heterogeneity in the time-varying reproduction number (Rt) during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BDBV) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as national-level estimates may not capture local variations in transmission.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study conducted a hierarchical Bayesian analysis of the 2026 BDBV outbreak across five provinces in the DRC, focusing on estimating Rt at national, provincial, and health-zone levels where sufficient case data was available.
analysis.methods: The researchers used a standard sliding-window estimator and a hierarchical Bayesian renewal model with partial pooling across spatial units, fitted by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (No-U-Turn Sampler) to account for sub-national variations in transmission.
analysis.main_results: Provincial estimates of Rt diverged from the national trend, with Ituri having a median of 0.91 (95% credible interval [CrI] 0.68 - 1.24), Nord-Kivu at 1.23 (0.87 - 1.72), and Haut-Uele at 1.79 (1.24 - 2.67). Health-zone analysis revealed further heterogeneity, with some zones showing declining transmission while others remained above the epidemic threshold.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the importance of sub-national analysis in understanding transmission dynamics, as they reveal significant local variations that a single national estimate might obscure.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results can inform targeted public health interventions by identifying specific zones with ongoing supercritical transmission, allowing for more effective resource allocation and outbreak control strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Aggregation at higher spatial levels may mask important local heterogeneity, and reliance on case volume for health-zone analysis limits the scope of detailed sub-national insights. The evidence strength is moderate, as the study addresses these limitations through explicit model checks and sensitivity analyses.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BDBV) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to assess sub-national heterogeneity in the time-varying reproduction number (Rt). National-level estimates suggested convergence near the epidemic threshold, but provincial estimates revealed significant variation, with some areas still experiencing supercritical transmission. Health-zone analysis further highlighted localized differences, showing that even within provinces, transmission intensity varied. The study used a hierarchical Bayesian renewal model with partial pooling and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to estimate Rt, addressing limitations in data reporting and model assumptions. The findings emphasize the need for localized surveillance and response strategies to effectively manage outbreaks. However, the study acknowledges that aggregation may obscure important heterogeneity, and the evidence strength is moderate due to these limitations.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估2026年布尼亚病毒病(BDBV)暴发在刚果民主共和国(DRC)的次国家级异质性,因为国家级估计可能无法捕捉传播的局部变化。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究对刚果民主共和国(DRC)五个省份的2026年BDBV 暴发进行了层次贝叶斯分析,重点是在有足够的病例数据的情况下估计国家级、省级和卫生区级别的Rt。
elements_zh.methods: 研究人员使用标准滑动窗口估计器和部分跨空间单位混合贝叶斯更新模型(通过哈密尔顿蒙特卡洛拟合,No-U-Turn采样器),以应对传播的次国家级变化。
elements_zh.main_results: 省级Rt估计值与国家级趋势存在差异,伊图里省的中位数为0.91(95%可信区间[CrI] 0.68 - 1.24),北基伍省为1.23(0.87 - 1.72),上乌埃勒省为1.79(1.24 - 2.67)。卫生区分析揭示了进一步的异质性,一些区传播下降,而其他区仍高于流行病阈值。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果强调了次国家级分析在理解传播动态中的重要性,因为它们揭示了单个国家级估计可能掩盖的显著局部差异。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果可以指导针对特定区的公共卫生干预措施,以识别传播仍处于超临界状态的具体区域,从而更有效地分配资源和控制暴发。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 在较高空间级别上的聚合可能会掩盖重要的局部异质性,而依赖于病例数量进行卫生区分析限制了获得详细的次国家级洞察力。证据强度为中等,通过明确的模型检查和敏感性分析解决了这些限制。

Provincial estimates diverged materially from the national trend: as of the week of 6 August 2026, Ituri, the outbreak's original epicentre, had a hierarchical median Rt of 0.91 (95% credible interval [CrI] 0.68 - 1.24), while Nord-Kivu (1.23, [0.87 - 1.72]) and Haut-Uele (1.79, [1.24 - 2.67]) remained above threshold. Health-zone disaggregation, feasible only in Ituri and Nord-Kivu given case volume, showed this provincial picture itself masked further heterogeneity: in Ituri, the zone where the outbreak began (Mongbwalu) had clearly declined (Rt 0.36, [0.17 - 0.74]) while the two largest zones by cumulative case count (Bunia, Rwampara) remained at or above threshold; in Nord-Kivu, elevated transmission was concentrated in a single zone (Katwa, Rt 1.39, [0.85 - 1.99]) while a comparably-sized zone (Butembo) had already declined (0.64, [0.23 - 1.38]). An initial disagreement between the sliding-window and hierarchical provincial estimates was traced to a data-reconstruction artefact (forward-filling, rather than interpolating, multi-day gaps in health-zone reporting) rather than a genuine methods disagreement, and resolved once corrected. The hierarchical model's dispersion structure, calibration, and sensitivity to the generation-interval assumption were each checked explicitly; a shared (non-province-specific) dispersion parameter was retained on the basis of negligible predictive difference (PSIS-LOO), the model achieved 95.0% pooled 95% posterior-predictive interval coverage, and the province ranking was unchanged across a generation-interval sensitivity grid (Spearman {rho} = 1.0). Aggregation masks meaningful heterogeneity in transmission intensity at every spatial resolution examined; response prioritisation based on a single national or even provincial Rt risks directing attention away from the specific zones where transmission remains supercritical.
papers.abstract_zh: 2026年布尼亚病毒病(BDBV)暴发在刚果民主共和国(DRC)的国家级估计表明,自2026年8月初以来,时间变化的再生数(Rt)估计值已接近流行病阈值,与独立的联合贝叶斯更新模型估计结果一致。然而,单一国家级Rt可能掩盖不同地区的流行病轨迹,特别是在包含五个省份的暴发中,这些省份从原始疫区的下降到新出现的前沿不一而足。我们使用标准滑动窗口(Cori)估计器和部分跨空间单位混合贝叶斯更新模型(通过哈密尔顿蒙特卡洛拟合,No-U-Turn采样器)在国家级、省级和允许的情况下在卫生区级别估计Rt。省级估计值与国家级趋势存在实质性差异:截至2026年8月6日那一周,原始疫区伊图里省的混合后中位数Rt为0.91(95%可信区间[CrI] 0.68 - 1.24),而北基伍省(1.23,[0.87 - 1.72])和上乌埃勒省(1.79,[1.24 - 2.67])仍高于阈值。由于病例数量有限,仅在伊图里省和北基伍省进行了卫生区分解,显示了省级图景下的进一步异质性:在伊图里省,暴发开始的地方(蒙加瓦卢)Rt已明显下降(0.36,[0.17 - 0.74]),而累计病例最多的两个区(布尼亚,鲁万帕拉)仍处于或高于阈值;在北基伍省,传播集中在单个区(卡特瓦,Rt 1.39,[0.85 - 1.99]),而一个同样大小的区(布特梅博)已下降(0.64,[0.23 - 1.38])。滑动窗口和省级混合估计之间的初始分歧归因于数据重构伪影(前向填充,而不是插值多日报告中的空白),而不是真正的方法分歧,并在修正后得到解决。混合模型的分散结构、校准和对世代间隔假设的敏感性均得到了明确检查;基于微不足道的预测差异(PSIS-LOO),保留了共享的非省份特定分散参数,模型实现了95.0%的95%后验预测区间覆盖率,并且在世代间隔敏感性网格中省份排名保持不变(Spearman {rho} = 1.0)。聚合可能会在每个空间分辨率下掩盖传播强度的实质性异质性;基于单一国家级或省级Rt的响应优先级可能会将注意力从传播仍处于超临界状态的具体区域转移开。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估2026年布尼亚病毒病(BDBV)暴发在刚果民主共和国(DRC)的次国家级异质性,因为国家级估计可能无法捕捉传播的局部变化。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究对刚果民主共和国(DRC)五个省份的2026年BDBV 暴发进行了层次贝叶斯分析,重点是在有足够的病例数据的情况下估计国家级、省级和卫生区级别的Rt。
analysis_zh.methods: 研究人员使用标准滑动窗口估计器和部分跨空间单位混合贝叶斯更新模型(通过哈密尔顿蒙特卡洛拟合,No-U-Turn采样器),以应对传播的次国家级变化。
analysis_zh.main_results: 省级Rt估计值与国家级趋势存在差异,伊图里省的中位数为0.91(95%可信区间[CrI] 0.68 - 1.24),北基伍省为1.23(0.87 - 1.72),上乌埃勒省为1.79(1.24 - 2.67)。卫生区分析揭示了进一步的异质性,一些区传播下降,而其他区仍高于流行病阈值。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果强调了次国家级分析在理解传播动态中的重要性,因为它们揭示了单个国家级估计可能掩盖的显著局部差异。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果可以指导针对特定区的公共卫生干预措施,以识别传播仍处于超临界状态的具体区域,从而更有效地分配资源和控制暴发。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 在较高空间级别上的聚合可能会掩盖重要的局部异质性,而依赖于病例数量进行卫生区分析限制了获得详细的次国家级洞察力。证据强度为中等,通过明确的模型检查和敏感性分析解决了这些限制。

papers.title: Discovering host-viral protein interactions in autophagy: A LIR discovery pipeline for identifying LC3-interacting region motifs in highly virulent viruses.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever virus (HFV) infections are highly fatal, posing a significant global pandemic threat as they continue to emerge in new locations. HFVs and other highly virulent viruses (HVVs), such as Nipah virus, exploit host cell pathways, including the conserved host autophagy pathway, to promote viral replication. The Atg8/microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 (LC3) proteins are necessary for autophagosome formation and maturation. Proteins interact with Atg8-family proteins through LC3-interacting region (LIR) motifs, which is a short linear motif (SLiM) found in intrinsically disordered regions of proteins. The presence of these motifs in viral components suggests they play a role in hijacking or evading the host autophagy pathway, yet the identification of functional LIR motifs in viral proteins remains limited. To address this gap, we developed the LIR Discovery Pipeline (LIR-DP) which integrates amino acid sequence pattern matching, with protein disorder prediction using IUPred3, and modeling with AlphaFold3. Using LIR-DP, we identified 43 putative LIR motifs in 166 proteins from 22 HVVs and predicted that 18 of these LIRs would be functional. In vitro and in cellulo laboratory experiments demonstrated that LIRs from the Marburg virus nucleoprotein, the Nipah virus phosphoprotein, the Ebola virus VP35, and the Rift Valley fever virus NSs protein bind to Atg8/LC3 family proteins. The aromatic amino acid in the first position of each LIR motif was found to be critical for these interactions. We provide evidence for the utility of the LIR-DP in identifying functional LIRs within HVV proteins which may provide valuable insight into the mechanism by which HVVs modulate the autophagy pathway during infection.

papers.abstract_zh: 出血热病毒(HFV)感染具有高致死率,构成了严重的全球疫情威胁,因为它们不断在新的地区出现。HFV 和其他高致病性病毒(HVV),如尼帕病毒,利用 宿主 细胞途径(包括保守的 宿主 自噬途径)来促进病毒复制。Atg8/微管相关蛋白 1 轻链 3(LC3)蛋白对于自噬泡的形成和成熟至关重要。蛋白质通过 LC3 相互作用区域(LIR)基序与 Atg8 家族蛋白相互作用,LIR 基序是蛋白质中不可溶区域发现的一种短线性基序(SLiM)。病毒成分中存在这些基序,表明它们可能在劫持或逃避 宿主 自噬途径中发挥作用,但病毒蛋白中功能性 LIR 基序的识别仍然有限。为了填补这一空白,我们开发了 LIR 发现管道(LIR-DP),该管道集成了氨基酸序列模式匹配、IUPred3 蛋白质无序性预测和 AlphaFold3 建模技术。使用 LIR-DP,我们在 22 种 HVV 的 166 种蛋白中发现了 43 个潜在的 LIR 基序,并预测其中 18 个 LIR 是功能性的。体外和细胞内实验室实验表明,马尔堡病毒核蛋白、尼帕病毒磷蛋白、埃博拉病毒 VP35 和裂谷热病毒 NSs 蛋白的 LIR 能够与 Atg8/LC3 家族蛋白结合。每个 LIR 基序中第一个位置的芳香族氨基酸对这些相互作用至关重要。我们提供了证据,证明 LIR-DP 在识别 HVV 蛋白中功能性 LIR 方面的有效性,这可能为 HVV 在感染期间如何调节自噬途径提供宝贵的见解。

papers.title: Evaluating the 7-1-7 Outbreak Response Metric: Modelling and Implementation Insights for Ebola, Measles, and Anthrax in Central and Eastern Uganda, 2025
papers.abstract: Introduction: Uganda’s recent progress in public health emergency preparedness underscores the relevance of the 7–1-7 framework (detection within 7 days, notification within 1 day, response within 7 days). Evidence on the incremental benefits of meeting these targets in resource-constrained settings remains limited. We modelled cases averted and cost-effectiveness of achieving 7–1-7 timelines for Sudan virus disease (SVD), measles, and anthrax in Uganda, and additionally explored more ambitious targets (3–1-4 and 1–1-1). Methods We used stochastic compartmental models to compare observed response time lines with hypothetical scenarios that meet 7–1-7 targets. Surveillance data from recent outbreaks informed the models. Cost-effectiveness was assessed using Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) averted and Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratios (ICERs). Additional simulations tested the impact of compressing timelines to 3–1-4 and 1–1-1 while keeping all other intervention parameters identical. Results Under the modelled 7–1-7 scenario, 133 SVD cases (47 deaths) and 1,409 DALYs would be averted, with an ICER of −17.46 USD/DALY (cost-saving). For measles, 81 cases and one death would be averted (ICER 83 USD/DALY). For anthrax, the framework would prevent three human cases (one death) and 50 animal cases (45 animal deaths), averting 734 DALYs, but would require an additional US$651,811 for livestock vaccination and carcass disposal. All ICERs fell below Uganda’s willingness-to-pay threshold (1,300 USD/DALY). Moving beyond 7–1-7 to 1–1-1 would avert an additional 55 SVD cases and 21 deaths, and 13 measles cases, at negligible incremental cost, demonstrating that even faster response yields substantial extra health gains. For anthrax, faster timelines beyond 7–1-7 produced only marginal benefits, confirming that vaccination coverage – not timeliness – is the dominant driver. Conclusion The 7–1-7 framework substantially reduces cases, deaths, and costs across three diverse diseases. Accelerating to 1–1-1 further amplifies these benefits for fast-spreading pathogens like Ebola and measles, but for slow zoonoses like anthrax, improving vaccination coverage remains paramount. Achieving these targets requires investments in rapid detection, contact tracing, vaccination, referral systems, and sustainable multi-sector financing.

papers.abstract_zh: 引言:乌干达在公共卫生紧急事件准备方面的最新进展凸显了7–1-7框架(7天内检测、1天内通报、7天内响应)的相关性。目前关于在资源有限环境中实现这些目标的增量效益的证据仍然有限。我们对乌干达实现7–1-7时间线的SVD(苏丹病毒病)、麻疹和炭疽病例数和成本效益进行了建模,并进一步探讨了更具雄心的目标(3–1-4和1–1-1)。方法:我们使用随机的分室模型,将观察到的响应时间线与假设符合7–1-7目标的场景进行比较。近期监测数据用于模型构建。成本效益评估采用避免的伤残调整生命年(DALYs)和增量成本效益比(ICERs)。此外,我们进行了额外的模拟,测试将时间线压缩至3–1-4和1–1-1时,其他干预参数保持不变的情况下所产生的影响。结果:在模拟的7–1-7情景下,可避免133例SVD病例(47例死亡)和1,409个DALYs,其ICER为−17.46 USD/DALY(成本节约)。对于麻疹,可避免81例病例和1例死亡(ICER 83 USD/DALY)。对于炭疽病,该框架可防止3例人类病例(1例死亡)和50例动物病例(45例动物死亡),避免734个DALYs,但需要额外651,811美元用于牲畜疫苗接种和尸体处理。所有ICER均低于乌干达的意愿支付阈值(1,300 USD/DALY)。超越7–1-7框架,采用1–1-1框架可额外避免55例SVD病例和21例死亡,以及13例麻疹病例,其增量成本微乎其微,表明即使更快的响应也能带来显著的额外健康收益。对于炭疽病,更快的时间线仅产生有限的效益,证实了疫苗接种覆盖率——而非响应速度——是主要驱动因素。结论:7–1-7框架在三种不同的疾病中显著减少了病例、死亡和成本。对于传播迅速的病原体如埃博拉病毒和麻疹,加速至1–1-1框架可进一步放大这些效益,但对于传播较慢的人兽共患病如炭疽病,提高疫苗接种覆盖率仍然是关键。实现这些目标需要在快速检测、接触追踪、疫苗接种、转诊系统和可持续的多部门资金投入方面进行投资。

papers.title: MHRN Roundtable Report: Social and Behavioural Science Priorities for Ebola Clinical Trials in DRC
papers.abstract: A large outbreak of the Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) was first identified in the Ituri Province in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in May 2026. This marked the DRC’s 17th Ebola outbreak overall and only the third known outbreak of this virus since its identification in Uganda in 2007. There are currently no licensed vaccines or therapeutics for BDBV, though several trials are planned and underway. DRC has been at the centre of major experimental Ebola vaccine, and therapeutic and diagnostic research over the past decade. Experience from the outbreak in North Kivu in 2018–20, the DRC-EB-001 trial of the Janssen two-dose vaccine, and more recent mpox vaccine trials has generated important lessons about rumour, mistrust, participant experience, protocol change, and the inclusion of vulnerable groups. A growing body of social science research shows that social and behavioural science (SBS) and risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) can strengthen trial operations when they are integrated from the beginning. This includes improving design and implementation, reducing the risk of coercion or misunderstanding, supporting local ethical deliberation, and identifying contextual factors that may otherwise undermine feasibility, recruitment, retention, and trust. Against this backdrop, the Multi-Hazard Research Network (MHRN) organised an online roundtable on 18 August 2026. The aim was to consolidate lessons learned from past SBS research in/on Ebola clinical trials and discuss current challenges with clinical trial design and rollout. The discussion brought together SBS researchers, trial implementers, RCCE specialists, and Ebola responders.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the need for integrating social and behavioural science (SBS) and risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) into Ebola clinical trials to improve their design and implementation.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a roundtable discussion held on 18 August 2026 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), bringing together SBS researchers, trial implementers, RCCE specialists, and Ebola responders.
analysis.methods: The methods involved a structured online roundtable discussion to consolidate lessons learned from past SBS research in Ebola clinical trials and to discuss current challenges with trial design and rollout.
analysis.main_results: The discussion highlighted important lessons from past outbreaks, including the impact of rumour, mistrust, participant experience, protocol changes, and the inclusion of vulnerable groups.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as demonstrating the value of integrating SBS and RCCE from the beginning of clinical trials to enhance their effectiveness and address contextual challenges.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform future Ebola clinical trials by emphasizing the importance of incorporating social and behavioural insights to improve feasibility, recruitment, retention, and trust.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a discussion format and does not include empirical data, but the evidence is strong due to the integration of multiple expert perspectives and prior research findings.

analysis.summary_en: This report outlines the importance of integrating social and behavioural science (SBS) and risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) into Ebola clinical trials. It highlights the need for these approaches to address challenges such as mistrust, rumour, and the inclusion of vulnerable groups, based on lessons from past outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The study was a roundtable discussion held on 18 August 2026, involving SBS researchers, trial implementers, RCCE specialists, and Ebola responders. The findings suggest that incorporating SBS and RCCE from the outset can improve trial design and implementation. The report emphasizes the significance of these insights for future Ebola trials, particularly in enhancing feasibility and trust. However, the study is limited to a discussion format and lacks empirical data, which may affect the strength of the evidence. The confidence in the findings is moderate due to the nature of the evidence and the absence of quantitative results.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在解决将社会与行为科学(SBS)和风险沟通与社区参与(RCCE)整合到埃博拉临床试验中的需求,以提高试验的设计和实施效果。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究是在刚果民主共和国(DRC)于2026年8月18日举行的一次圆桌会议,汇集了社会与行为科学研究人员、试验实施人员、风险沟通与社区参与专家以及埃博拉应对人员。

elements_zh.main_results: 讨论强调了过去疫情中的重要经验教训,包括谣言、不信任、参与者体验、方案变更以及脆弱群体纳入的影响。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为表明,从临床试验开始阶段就整合社会与行为科学(SBS)和风险沟通与社区参与(RCCE)对于提高试验效果和应对背景挑战具有重要价值。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为未来的埃博拉临床试验提供信息,强调将社会与行为科学见解纳入其中对于提高可行性、招募、保留和信任的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅限于讨论形式,不包含实证数据,但由于整合了多种专家观点和以往研究结果,其证据是强有力的。

papers.abstract_zh: 2026年5月,刚果民主共和国(DRC)的伊图里省首次发现了邦迪布古埃博拉病毒(BDBV)的大规模暴发。这标志着DRC自2007年该病毒在乌干达被鉴定以来的第17次埃博拉病毒暴发,也是该病毒第三次已知的暴发。目前尚无针对BDBV的获批抗病毒药物或治疗药物,尽管已有多个试验计划并正在进行中。过去十年中,DRC一直是重大实验性埃博拉病毒药物、治疗和诊断研究的中心。从2018–20年北基伏地区的暴发、DRC-EB-001试验中詹森双剂量疫苗的试验,以及最近的猴痘病毒试验中获得的经验,为理解谣言、不信任、参与者体验、方案变更以及脆弱群体的纳入提供了重要启示。越来越多的社会科学研究表明,当社会和行为科学(SBS)和风险沟通与社区参与(RCCE)从一开始就整合到试验中时,可以增强试验的运行效果。这包括改进试验设计和实施,降低胁迫或误解的风险,支持本地伦理讨论,并识别可能影响试验可行性、招募、保留和信任的背景因素。在此背景下,多灾害研究网络(MHRN)于2026年8月18日组织了一次在线圆桌会议。会议旨在总结过去埃博拉临床试验中社会行为科学研究的经验,并讨论当前临床试验设计和实施中的挑战。讨论汇集了社会行为科学研究人员、试验实施人员、风险沟通与社区参与专家以及埃博拉应对人员。

papers.title: Optimal control metapopulation models for the West Africa Ebola epidemic and their nonstandard finite difference discretizations
papers.abstract: The 2014-2016 Ebola Virus disease (EVD) outbreak came with an unprecedented challenge. It simultaneously arose in three different countries with considerable inbound and outbound travels. This led the World Health Organization (WHO) to suggest implementing exit screening of travelers at their borders. In addition to this measure, some countries accounted for entry screening and/or vaccination to curb the disease. In this paper, we consider two optimal controls for patch models in which other interventions supplement exit screening. The first problem is defined through the exit and entry screenings of travelers. The second involves the combination of exit screening and vaccination interventions. We prove the well-posedness of both optimal control problems. For each problem, we construct a new Nonstandard Finite Difference Forward-Backward-Sweep-Method, which preserves the dynamics of the continuous model. Numerical simulations that support the theory are provided. They also suggest that vaccination alone is effective in reducing the disease burden.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 2014-2016年的埃博拉病毒病(EVD)疫情带来了前所未有的挑战。该疫情同时出现在三个不同的国家,且这些国家之间有大量人员往来,这促使世界卫生组织(WHO)建议在其边境对旅行者进行出境筛查。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本文考虑了两种针对补充分出筛查的元种群模型的最优控制策略。
elements_zh.methods: 我们证明了这两个最优控制问题的适定性,并构建了一种新的非标准有限差分前向-后向扫描方法,该方法保留了连续模型的动力学特性。提供了支持理论的数值模拟。
elements_zh.main_results: 数值模拟表明,仅通过疫苗接种即可有效降低疾病负担。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 本文引入了两种针对元种群模型的最优控制问题,并开发了一种新的数值方法来解决这些问题,提供了对不同干预措施有效性的见解。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为未来埃博拉病毒病的最优控制策略设计提供参考,特别是关注出境筛查与疫苗接种的结合。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究基于数学模型和模拟,可能无法完全反映现实世界中的复杂情况。证据强度中等。

analysis_en.study_design_and_population: This paper considers two optimal controls for patch models in which other interventions supplement exit screening.
analysis_en.methods: We prove the well-posedness of both optimal control problems and construct a new Nonstandard Finite Difference Forward-Backward-Sweep-Method, which preserves the dynamics of the continuous model. Numerical simulations that support the theory are provided.
analysis_en.main_results: The numerical simulations suggest that vaccination alone is effective in reducing the disease burden.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The paper introduces two optimal control problems for patch models and develops a new numerical method to solve them, providing insights into the effectiveness of different interventions.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the design of optimal control strategies for future outbreaks, particularly focusing on the combination of exit screening and vaccination.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on mathematical models and simulations, which may not fully capture the complexities of real-world scenarios. The evidence strength is moderate.

papers.title_zh: 西非埃博拉疫情的最优控制元种群模型及其非标准有限差分离散化方法
papers.source_body_en: The 2014-2016 Ebola Virus disease (EVD) outbreak came with an unprecedented challenge. It simultaneously arose in three different countries with considerable inbound and outbound travels. This led the World Health Organization (WHO) to suggest implementing exit screening of travelers at their borders. In addition to this measure, some countries accounted for entry screening and/or vaccination to curb the disease. In this paper, we consider two optimal controls for patch models in which other interventions supplement exit screening. The first problem is defined through the exit and entry screenings of travelers. The second involves the combination of exit screening and vaccination interventions. We prove the well-posedness of both optimal control problems. For each problem, we construct a new Nonstandard Finite Difference Forward-Backward-Sweep-Method, which preserves the dynamics of the continuous model. Numerical simulations that support the theory are provided. They also suggest that vaccination alone is effective in reducing the disease burden.
papers.abstract_zh: 2014-2016年的埃博拉病毒病(EVD)疫情带来了前所未有的挑战。该疫情同时出现在三个不同的国家,且这些国家之间有大量人员往来。这促使世界卫生组织(WHO)建议在其边境对旅行者进行出境筛查。除了这一措施外,一些国家还实施了入境筛查和/或疫苗接种以控制该疾病。本文考虑了两种针对补充分出筛查的元种群模型的最优控制策略。第一个问题涉及对旅行者进行出境和入境筛查,第二个问题则涉及将出境筛查与疫苗接种相结合。我们证明了这两个最优控制问题的适定性。对于每个问题,我们构建了一种新的非标准有限差分前向-后向扫描方法,该方法保留了连续模型的动力学特性。提供了支持理论的数值模拟,它们还表明,仅通过疫苗接种即可有效降低疾病负担。
papers.summary_zh: 2014-2016年的埃博拉病毒病(EVD)疫情带来了前所未有的挑战。该疫情同时出现在三个不同的国家,且这些国家之间有大量人员往来。这促使世界卫生组织(WHO)建议在其边境对旅行者进行出境筛查。除了这一措施外,一些国家还实施了入境筛查和/或疫苗接种以控制该疾病。本文考虑了两种针对补充分出筛查的元种群模型的最优控制策略。第一个问题涉及对旅行者进行出境和入境筛查,第二个问题则涉及将出境筛查与疫苗接种相结合。我们证明了这两个最优控制问题的适定性。对于每个问题,我们构建了一种新的非标准有限差分前向-后向扫描方法,该方法保留了连续模型的动力学特性。提供了支持理论的数值模拟,它们还表明,仅通过疫苗接种即可有效降低疾病负担。

analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本文考虑了两种针对补充分出筛查的元种群模型的最优控制策略。
analysis_zh.methods: 我们证明了这两个最优控制问题的适定性,并构建了一种新的非标准有限差分前向-后向扫描方法,该方法保留了连续模型的动力学特性。提供了支持理论的数值模拟。
analysis_zh.main_results: 数值模拟表明,仅通过疫苗接种即可有效降低疾病负担。

analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为未来埃博拉病毒病的最优控制策略设计提供参考,特别是关注出境筛查与疫苗接种的结合。

papers.title: First mRNA‐based flu vaccine wins US approval, Moderna’s Ebola candidate reaches the clinic, and early‐phase cancer vaccine trials broaden across personalized and off‐the‐shelf platforms
papers.abstract: The US FDA approved the first mRNA-based influenza vaccine, clearing the way for messenger RNA technology to move into a second major indication beyond COVID-19, while Moderna dosed the first participants in its own mRNA candidate against Bundibugyo ebolavirus as the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continued. Mpox vaccine access widened to children as young as two in the European Union, a six-valent Lyme disease vaccine advanced toward EU review, and a cluster of early-phase trials opened for personalized and off-the-shelf cancer vaccine candidates spanning lung, breast, esophagogastric, and pancreatic cancer.

papers.source_body_en: The US FDA approved the first mRNA-based influenza vaccine, clearing the way for messenger RNA technology to move into a second major indication beyond COVID-19, while Moderna dosed the first participants in its own mRNA candidate against Bundibugyo ebolavirus as the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continued. Mpox vaccine access widened to children as young as two in the European Union, a six-valent Lyme disease vaccine advanced toward EU review, and a cluster of early-phase trials opened for personalized and off-the-shelf cancer vaccine candidates spanning lung, breast, esophagogastric, and pancreatic cancer.
papers.abstract_zh: 美国食品药品监督管理局批准了首款基于mRNA技术的流感疫苗疫苗,为信使RNA技术在COVID-19之外进入第二个主要适应症领域铺平了道路。与此同时,Moderna公司为其针对邦迪布吉奥埃博拉病毒的mRNA候选疫苗接种了首批受试者,该疫苗在刚果民主共和国的暴发试验继续进行。欧盟将Mpox疫苗疫苗的接种范围扩大到两岁以下儿童,一种六价莱姆病疫苗疫苗已进入欧盟审查阶段,同时还有一批早期临床试验启动,涉及个性化和现成可用的癌症疫苗疫苗候选药物,涵盖肺癌、乳腺癌、食管胃癌和胰腺癌。
papers.summary_zh: 美国食品药品监督管理局批准了首款基于mRNA技术的流感疫苗疫苗,为信使RNA技术在COVID-19之外进入第二个主要适应症领域铺平了道路。与此同时,Moderna公司为其针对邦迪布吉奥埃博拉病毒的mRNA候选疫苗接种了首批受试者,该疫苗在刚果民主共和国的暴发试验继续进行。欧盟将Mpox疫苗疫苗的接种范围扩大到两岁以下儿童,一种六价莱姆病疫苗疫苗已进入欧盟审查阶段,同时还有一批早期临床试验启动,涉及个性化和现成可用的癌症疫苗疫苗候选药物,涵盖肺癌、乳腺癌、食管胃癌和胰腺癌。

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo + 9 more IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 17 (31 August to 6 September 2026) Format Situation Report Source IOM Posted 11 Sep 2026 Originally published 11 Sep 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 1.46 MB) SITUATION OVERVIEW 30,560,048 Health screenings supported at PoEs/PoCs 230 PoEs/PoCs supported across affected and at-risk countries 26,500,916 Individuals reached through RCCE activities According to the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), over 6,200 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) had been reported as of 1 September and more than 3,000 confirmed deaths. The outbreak is unfolding against the backdrop of a longstanding triple crisis in eastern DRC, where conflict, displacement and health risks converge, leaving internally displaced persons (IDPs) and mobile populations at heightened risk. Over 50 IOM-managed IDP sites in eastern DRC, located in the areas of Ituri and North Kivu, are impacted by the outbreak. Inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), health and shelter services accelerate risks of disease transmission and compound vulnerabilities, impacting the safety and protection of displaced, mobile and host communities. Over 10 per cent of the journeys originating in affected areas of Ituri Province led to a zone without new cases, as per latest data from IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM). Nearly 4 per cent of travellers leave Ituri for other locations across DRC, including Kinshasa, as well as to other countries, including Uganda and Tanzania. At the same time, data indicates a total of 171 fatalities intercepted at points of control (PoCs) – highlighting the continued importance of expanding health operations across DRC to effectively detect, prevent and respond to potential new cases. Given ongoing transmission in Haut-Uélé and Bas-Uélé Provinces in DRC, bordering the prefectures of Haut-Mbomou and Mbomou in CAR, there remains a high risk of cross-border spread. Porous borders, informal crossings and frequent cross-border population movements linked to trade, family ties, health-care-seeking behaviours, livelihoods, displacement and insecurity may facilitate transmission and compound existing humanitarian vulnerabilities. Investments in preparedness, including strengthening screening, community and event-based surveillance, risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) and infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, alongside strengthening data systems and pre-positioning of essential supplies at priority border locations, are therefore urgently required to support early detection and mitigate cross-border spread. In line with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) systemwide scale-up activation for infectious disease events, IOM has scaled up its response, particularly at points of entry (PoEs), PoCs and in displacement sites, enabling enhanced surge support, operational capacity and coordination across affected countries. IOM’s response continues to focus on Priority 1a countries, DRC and Uganda, where outbreak response and enhanced preparedness activities remain ongoing and Priority 1b countries, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, which face an elevated risk of cross-border transmission. Preparedness interventions are also implemented in other at-risk countries across the region, including Priority 2 countries, Angola, the Central African Republic (CAR), Ethiopia, Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, the United Republic of Tanzania and Zambia, to strengthen readiness and enhance regional health security, while supporting continent-wide efforts, particularly as co-lead of the PoE technical working group at the continental level. news.title_zh: IOM:多国爆发邦迪布古病毒病(BVD)疫情 - 第17期情况报告(2026年8月31日至9月6日) - ReliefWeb
news.source_body_en: The IOM Situation Report No. 17 details a multi-country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with data as of 1 September 2026. Over 6,200 confirmed cases and more than 3,000 confirmed deaths have been reported, primarily in the provinces of Haut-Uélé and Bas-Uélé, which border the Central African Republic (CAR). The outbreak is affecting internally displaced persons (IDPs), mobile populations, and host communities in eastern DRC, particularly in Ituri and North Kivu, where over 50 IOM-managed IDP sites are impacted. The report highlights the risk of cross-border spread due to porous borders and frequent population movements between DRC and neighboring countries like Uganda and Tanzania. IOM has intensified its response at points of entry (PoEs), points of control (PoCs), and displacement sites to enhance detection and prevention efforts. The outbreak remains under active investigation, with ongoing health operations aimed at mitigating further transmission.
news.content_zh: IOM第17期情况报告详细描述了2026年9月1日为止在刚果民主共和国(DRC)发生的多国邦迪布古病毒病(BVD)疫情。截至2026年9月1日,已报告超过6,200例确诊病例和超过3,000例死亡病例,主要集中在与中非共和国(CAR)接壤的上乌 ele 和下乌 ele 省。该疫情正在影响刚果民主共和国东部的内部流离失所者(IDPs)、流动人口以及特定社区,特别是在Ituri和北基伏省,超过50个由IOM管理的IDP站点受到影响。报告指出,由于边境开放和DRC与邻国如乌干达和坦桑尼亚之间频繁的人口流动,存在跨境传播的风险。IOM已加强在入境点(PoEs)、控制点(PoCs)和流离失所者安置点的响应,以提高检测和预防能力。该疫情仍处于积极调查中,正在进行的健康行动旨在减少进一步传播的风险。

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo DRC — Ituri: Population Flow Monitoring Dashboard in the Context of the Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) Response, Week 36 (August - September 2026) Format Infographic Source IOM Posted 14 Sep 2026 Originally published 14 Sep 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Infographic (PDF | 6 MB) This weekly DTM DRC Flow Monitoring dashboard provides an overview of mobility dynamics observed in Ituri Province in the context of the Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) response. It presents key trends in traveller movements recorded at active Flow Monitoring Points, as well as an analysis of movements linked to health zones affected by active disease transmission. Data were collected from 31 August to 6 September 2026 at seven active points of control. A total of 80,090 travellers were counted and 4,466 individual interviews were conducted to analyse travel routes, traveller profiles, and movements between health zones within and beyond the province. Results indicate that 86 per cent of journeys crossed a health zone boundary, while 5 per cent of travellers left Ituri Province during the reporting period. This dashboard will be updated on a weekly basis to provide regular information on mobility trends in the context of the EVD response. As the monitoring network expands, geographical coverage will be progressively strengthened to enhance population movement monitoring and support outbreak response activities. Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo DRC — Ituri: Population Flow Monitoring Dashboard in the Context of the Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) Response, Week 36 (August - September 2026) Format Infographic Source IOM Posted 14 Sep 2026 Originally published 14 Sep 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Infographic (PDF | 6 MB) This weekly DTM DRC Flow Monitoring dashboard provides an overview of mobility dynamics observed in Ituri Province in the context of the Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) response. It presents key trends in traveller movements recorded at active Flow Monitoring Points, as well as an analysis of movements linked to health zones affected by active disease transmission. Data were collected from 31 August to 6 September 2026 at seven active points of control. A total of 80,090 travellers were counted and 4,466 individual interviews were conducted to analyse travel routes, traveller profiles, and movements between health zones within and beyond the province. Results indicate that 86 per cent of journeys crossed a health zone boundary, while 5 per cent of travellers left Ituri Province during the reporting period. This dashboard will be updated on a weekly basis to provide regular information on mobility trends in the context of the EVD response. As the monitoring network expands, geographical coverage will be progressively strengthened to enhance population movement monitoring and support outbreak response activities. To date, no cases of Ebola disease have been confirmed in the United States because of this outbreak. The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low. Outbreak overview Risk to the United States To date, no Ebola cases associated with this outbreak have been reported in the United States. The likelihood of Ebola spreading to the United States is considered very low. If a case was diagnosed in the United States, the risk of Ebola spreading in the United States is also low due to the strength of our public health system and infection control measures. CDC is responding to an outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). This outbreak is spreading substantially faster than previous Ebola outbreaks and is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, a type of Ebola virus. In DRC, cases have been confirmed in Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), Sud-Ubangi (South Ubangi), and Tshopo provinces. This is the 17th outbreak of Ebola in DRC. This Ebola outbreak surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation. In comparison, the 2018 Ebola outbreak in DRC took approximately 235 days to reach more than 1,000 cases. South Kivu has reported no confirmed cases since May 29. Uganda also reported cases of Ebola at the same time DRC declared an outbreak. Uganda reported 21 confirmed and probable cases and 3 deaths. Response challenges The response to this outbreak is challenging due to a number of complex circumstances in the region. Limited health infrastructure, including limited access to healthcare, diagnostic and laboratory services, infection prevention and control supplies, and other basic services make stopping this outbreak more difficult. Ongoing conflict in the area where the outbreak is occurring creates security issues and complicates contact tracing and infection prevention and control. Violence against healthcare workers and shortages of personal protective equipment are leading to healthcare workers becoming infected while treating patients. Frequent population movement and cross-border travel increase the risk of spread to Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, and to other areas. Lack of trust in the government and misinformation make communicating about Ebola more difficult. To reduce the risk of Ebola importation into the United States, U.S. entry for travelers who were recently in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is temporarily restricted. Travelers, including Americans, who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight will not be allowed to board commercial flights with U.S. destinations. All U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been in DRC should plan to remain outside DRC for 21 days before entering the United States. This includes all passengers with an intermediate stop in DRC or on multi-stop itineraries via DRC regardless of whether they disembark or stay on the airplane. U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been present in Uganda or South Sudan (and not present in DRC) within 21 days of arrival in the United States must only enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. This process is in addition to CDC's Order, under 42 CFR 71.40, that continued the temporary entry restrictions to the United States for certain categories of travelers after they were in DRC, Uganda, or South Sudan. CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu (North Kivu) provinces and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces in DRC. Travelers to other parts of DRC or Uganda should take enhanced precautions to avoid Ebola exposure and monitor for symptoms while traveling and for 21 days after leaving. The DRC MoH does not include probable cases in their official reporting. Suspected cases and suspected deaths in DRC have been temporarily excluded from the count pending ongoing investigations and data standardization. The Uganda MoH does not include suspected cases in their official reporting. Map of affected areas View LargerDownload To date, the Ebola disease outbreak in DRC has been confirmed in Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), Sud-Ubangi (South Ubangi), and Tshopo provinces. Cases related to the DRC outbreak also have been reported in Uganda's capital of Kampala. CDC response CDC is working internationally and domestically to respond to this outbreak and prevent Ebola from entering the United States. About 500 people at CDC are involved in responding to the outbreak, including more than 120 people deployed to the affected countries. Español What to know Travel from Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC): Travelers, including U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals, who have been in DRC within 21 days before departure will not be allowed to board commercial flights with U.S. destinations. These travelers should plan to remain outside the United States for at least 21 days after they leave DRC. If they have been in outbreak-affected provinces in DRC, they may be subject to additional travel requirements from local authorities before they leave DRC. Travel from Uganda or South Sudan: U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been present in Uganda or South Sudan (and not present in DRC) within 21 days before arrival in the United States will have their air travel routed through designated U.S. airports for public health entry screening. Background To reduce the risk of Ebola importation into the United States, U.S. entry for travelers who were recently in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is temporarily restricted. Travelers, including Americans, who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight will not be allowed to board commercial flights with U.S. destinations. All U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been in DRC should plan to remain outside DRC for 21 days before entering the United States. This includes all passengers with an intermediate stop in DRC or on multi-stop itineraries via DRC regardless of whether they disembark or stay on the airplane. U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been present in Uganda or South Sudan (and not present in DRC) within 21 days of arrival in the United States must only enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. This process is in addition to CDC's Order, under 42 CFR 71.40, that continued the temporary entry restrictions to the United States for certain categories of travelers after they were in DRC, Uganda, or South Sudan. More information for travelers Americans who need consular assistance can visit Additional Consular Information for Americans Regarding the Ebola Outbreak, or call the Department of State: From the U.S. and Canada: +1-888-407-4747 From all other locations: +1-202-501-4444 For travelers who have been outside of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, or South Sudan for more than 21 days and need assistance with a public health travel restriction, please contact Ebola-Travel-HELP@hq.dhs.gov. Keep Reading Order: Suspending the Right to Introduce Certain Persons from Countries Where a Quarantinable Communicable Disease Exists Before you travel to the U.S. Travel from DRC The United States has temporary travel restrictions for people, including U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals, who have recently been in DRC. If you have been in DRC during the previous 21 days: You will not be permitted to board a commercial flight to the United States until 21 days have passed since you left DRC. This applies even if you were on an airplane that stopped at an airport in DRC regardless of whether you disembarked or stayed on the airplane. You should plan to remain outside the United States until at least 21 days have passed since you left DRC. IMPORTANT Travelers who have been in outbreak provinces in the DRC may have specific travel requirements from local DRC authorities. Always check entry requirements of any country you plan to visit during the 21 days after you leave DRC. Use this graphic as a reference for when you can return to the United States. View Larger After leaving the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), travelers must remain outside the United States for 21 days. They may return to the United States beginning on Day 22. Travel from South Sudan or Uganda The United States has temporary travel restrictions for certain travelers, including U.S. lawful permanent residents (Green Card holders), who have recently been in Uganda or South Sudan. Travel by U.S. citizens and nationals who have been in South Sudan or Uganda is not restricted. For travelers who are permitted to enter the United States: Your travel will be rerouted to a designated U.S. airport for public health entry screening. This requirement applies even if you only traveled through South Sudan or Uganda on a connecting flight. Airlines will work with affected travelers to rebook flights, if needed. After You Arrive in the U.S. Travelers who have been in South Sudan or Uganda in the past 21 days and are permitted to enter the U.S. will undergo public health entry screening at one of the following U.S. airports: Washington-Dulles International Airport (IAD) outside Washington, D.C. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) in Atlanta, Georgia John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in New York, New York NOTE: Travelers who were in DRC, South Sudan, or Uganda more than 21 days before traveling to the United States will not need to undergo public health entry screening. During entry screening, travelers will: Be escorted to a screening area Complete a brief questionnaire about travel history and symptoms, if any Have their temperature checked Be observed for signs of illness by CDC staff Be enrolled in automated text messages from CDC to remind them to monitor their health for 21 days after they left the affected country. Some travelers will have an additional public health assessment based on their area of travel and activities while in the affected country. CDC will also share travelers' contact information with state or local public health authorities, as needed, for follow-up and support. If you do not have symptoms You will receive information about monitoring your health for 21 days after leaving the affected country. Most travelers without symptoms will continue to their final destination after public health entry screening. If you have symptoms If you have a fever or other symptoms consistent with Ebola, a CDC public health medical officer will conduct an additional evaluation. If Ebola is suspected, you will be transferred to a hospital for medical evaluation, isolation, and care. Steps to take after travel Monitor your health Monitor your health for 21 days after you leave DRC,* South Sudan or Uganda. After you arrive in the U.S., CDC will send you automated text messages reminding you to watch for symptoms and to take action if you get sick. Take your temperature If you were in DRC, take your temperature every day and again if you feel sick. If you were in South Sudan or Uganda, take your temperature if you feel sick. Watch for symptoms Watch for possible symptoms of Ebola such as fever (100.4°F/38°C or higher) or feeling feverish, headache or body aches, rash, weakness or tiredness, sore throat, diarrhea, vomiting, stomach pain, or unexplained bleeding or bruising (a late stage of illness). *People who have been granted an exception to travel to the United States. Travel During Your Monitoring Period CDC recommends that you remain in the United States and avoid international travel and cruise ship travel during your 21-day monitoring period. If you are in the U.S. and plan to travel domestically or internationally while you are being monitored, notify your health department before you leave. If you have been in DRC and leave the United States before completing the 21-day period, you will not be permitted to return until 21 days have passed since you left DRC. What to do if you get sick If you develop any signs or symptoms that might be Ebola: Separate yourself from others (isolate). Stay in a room by yourself and don't share a bathroom with others. Call your local health department (if you are in the United States) or health officials where you are located for advice about medical care. Tell the health department about your recent travel from a country with risk of Ebola and your symptoms. They can identify the best healthcare facility for you to go to, if needed. Health department staff can also help the facility prepare to provide care for you and take any health precautions needed. Follow all their instructions. Do not travel while sick. Travel only when you have been cleared by a doctor or health official. If you need urgent medical care and you can't reach your health department right away Call a healthcare provider. If you can't reach a healthcare provider, call 911. Tell them your symptoms and that you were recently in a country with risk of Ebola. Calling ahead before going to a healthcare facility helps the facility prepare for your arrival, including contacting the health department and taking any precautions needed. Ireland Politics Scotland Scotland Politics Wales Wales Politics Africa Asia China India Australia Europe Latin America Middle East In Pictures BBC InDepth BBC Verify Sport Business World of Business Technology of Business NYSE Opening Bell Technology Watch Documentaries Artificial Intelligence Intelligence Revolution AI v the Mind Tech Now Health Watch Documentaries Culture Watch Documentaries Film & TV Music Art & Design Style Books Entertainment News Arts Watch Documentaries Arts in Motion Travel Watch Documentaries Destinations Africa Antarctica Asia Australia and Pacific Caribbean & Bermuda Central America Europe Middle East North America South America World’s Table Culture & Experiences Adventures The SpeciaList To the Ends of the Earth Earth Watch Documentaries Science Natural Wonders Climate Solutions Sustainable Business Green Living Audio Podcast Categories Radio Audio FAQs Video Watch Documentaries BBC Maestro Discover the World Live Live News Live Sport Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 7 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google James Gallagher,Health and science correspondentand Emery Makumeno,BBC Africa, Kinshasa Reuters The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is now the deadliest of the 17 the country has faced as it continues to spread. United Nations experts have described it as the fastest growing outbreak on record in terms of new infections. Getting the spread of the deadly virus under control is challenging because it involves a rare species of Ebola for which there is no vaccine - though some are being tested - and the epicentre is in an area affected by conflict. Congolese Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba has said that there are "encouraging signs" that control measures are working as the daily number of new infections is falling, but the World Health Organization (WHO) has cautioned that it is too early to confidently say the spread of the virus has passed its peak. What is Ebola and what are the symptoms? Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus. Ebola viruses normally infect animals, typically fruit bats, but outbreaks among humans can sometimes start when people eat or handle infected animals. It takes two to 21 days for symptoms to appear. They come on suddenly and start like the flu or malaria, with fever, headache and tiredness. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. Ebola outbreaks used to be small and contained to remote rural areas. However, urbanisation is pushing larger populations closer to these natural reservoirs of Ebola and increasing the risk of transmission. Why is this Ebola outbreak different and is there a vaccine? This outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which had not been seen for over a decade. Named after a district in Uganda where it was first detected, Bundibugyo has only caused two previous outbreaks - in 2007 and 2012. One study showed that it killed about a third of those infected, far less than the more common Zaire (66.6%) and Sudan (48.5%) species. About 48% of those known to have been infected in the current outbreak have died. Initial blood tests for Ebola in the affected areas were negative as they were designed to identify the more common form of the disease. In July, the UK's medicines regulator, the MHRA, said it had given permission for the first human trials of a vaccine for Bundibugyo to go ahead. It was created by a team from the University of Oxford based on the same technology used in the Oxford-AstraZeneca Covid vaccine. It took scientists just eight weeks to develop the new jab after plugging in genetic code from the Bundibugyo species of Ebola. The vaccine is being tested on 50 volunteers from Oxford aged 18 to 55 to see whether it triggers the correct antibody response without causing significant side effects. Three other groups are also developing different vaccines for Bundibugyo although they have not yet entered clinical trials. While treatments are available for other species of the Ebola virus, no drugs have been specifically approved to treat those infected with Bundibugyo. DR Congo is currently preparing to roll out the Ervebo vaccine - which helps protect against the Zaïre species of Ebola - as part of a trial to see if it is effective against the Bundibugyo species. The WHO is also sponsoring a separate clinical trial in the country to see whether two existing antiviral therapies can improve survival rates. The two drugs selected as the most promising are an experimental monoclonal antibody called MBP134 and remdesivir, an injection into a vein, which is also used to treat Covid. A further complication is that the outbreak is taking place in a conflict zone, with a quarter of million people displaced from their homes and people moving across porous borders into neighbouring countries. Recovery of Ebola patients offers rare moments of joy at epicentre of outbreak How health workers in DR Congo are treating Ebola and staying safe 'Speed, money and compassion' - lessons from an Ebola survivor and other experts How did the current Ebola outbreak start? The first known case was a nurse who developed symptoms on 24 April, which means the virus had been spreading undetected for weeks. The nurse died in Bunia, the capital of eastern DR Congo's Ituri province, according to Congolese Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba. The victim's body was repatriated to Mongbwalu. Kamba said one of the reasons the virus spread so quickly was the number of people exposed to the body during the funeral ceremony. But researchers believe that it may have been spreading since February but it was initially misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid. 'I buried my parents one day after the other' - Ebola mourners learn how to grieve safely How many Ebola cases have been reported and where are they? On 15 September, officials said there had been 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 confirmed deaths from the virus in DR Congo. There have also been 1,700 recoveries from Ebola so far, including four nurses whose discharge from hospital was celebrated at a special ceremony. Ituri province is the epicentre of this outbreak and accounts for the vast majority of confirmed infections. Why DR Congo's Ebola outbreak is so hard to stop Cases have also been confirmed in North Kivu (714) and South Kivu (3), provinces partly controlled by the rebel AFC-M23 alliance. These discoveries signalled the outbreak's spread from its epicentre. On 11 September the Congolese authorities confirmed that a case had been found in a seventh province, South-Ubangi, which borders the Central African Republic. The last patient being treated for Ebola in neighbouring Uganda was discharged from hospital on 16 July. Up to that point, the country had recorded 20 confirmed cases - with most having travelled from DR Congo - and two deaths. Uganda announced it was Ebola-free on 28 July and on 27 August it passed the 42-day mark from when the last patient recovered, the international standard for when an Ebola outbreak can be declared over. What is being done in DR Congo to tackle the current Ebola outbreak? Getty Images The WHO and Congolese health authorities are urging residents to follow preventative measures to help limit the spread of Ebola Mass gatherings have been banned in provinces with confirmed cases. The capital city, Kinshasa - which has no confirmed cases and is located some 1,800 km (1,100) miles from the outbreak - has also been ordered to ban mass gatherings. The government has now established four laboratories in Ituri - in Bunia, Mongbwalu, Beni and Aru - which can test blood samples for Bundibugyo and deliver results within 24 hours, removing earlier delays. Surveillance systems, contact tracing and the treatment infrastructure, with dedicated centres in several affected towns, have also been expanded, according to the health minister. The WHO has dedicated $3.9m (£2.9m) to tackling the outbreak, while Africa CDC has announced a $319m budget. A toll-free number, 151, has been provided for reporting symptoms and people are being reminded to: avoid contact with bodies of people who died with symptoms, or with dead animals not eat raw meat, as undercooked food may transmit the virus practise social distancing. How have the rebels responded to the latest Ebola outbreak? The AFC-M23 group has created an Ebola response team in an effort to prevent transmissions in the areas it controls. In late June, the rebel authorities had declared their zones Ebola-free, but introduced new restrictions in August, following two travellers testing positive in North Kivu. Shared taxis and passenger boats between government-held and rebel-held areas of the province, have been suspended, highlighting the hostilities between the two sides. The region's Ebola response co-ordinator Dr Freddy Kaniki, told the BBC in July that while UN agencies such as the WHO and Unicef - for children - had been helping, there has been no co-ordination with the Congolese government. What's the fighting in DR Congo all about? Trump's 'historic' peace deal for DR Congo shattered after rebels seize key city What are Rwanda and other countries doing about the Ebola outbreak? Rwanda closed its borders with DR Congo earlier on in the outbreak. According to Congolese media, authorities began to reopen parts of the border late in June following a lull in local infections. Uganda has temporarily suspended flights, buses and all other public transport crossing the border with DR Congo. Several other African countries have tightened border screenings and bolstered health facilities. The US has extended travel restrictions on its citizens who have been to DR Congo. Anyone who wants to return home must spend 21 days in a third country before being allowed into America. Go to BBCAfrica.com for more news from the African continent. Britannica Editors Last updated Sep. 11, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Viewed through an electron microscope, ebolaviruses appear as long filaments, sometimes branched or intertwined. The virion (virus particle) contains one molecule of noninfectious single-stranded RNA (ribonucleic acid). It is not known how the viruses attack cells; it has been postulated that they produce proteins that suppress the immune system, allowing reproduction of virus to continue unhindered. Viral hemorrhagic fevers similar to Ebola typically are carried by arthropods and rodents, but the natural reservoirs for ebolaviruses are yet to be discovered. Among the suspected reservoirs for Ebola are bats, primates, rodents, and insects that inhabit tropical forests in Africa and Asia. Ebola can be transmitted through contact with infected blood and bodily fluids as well as through contact with surfaces or objects contaminated by those fluids. The virus has also been detected in the organs of patients after recovery from the fever. In men, the virus may remain infectious in semen for as long as two months following return to health. Unsanitary conditions and lack of adequate medical supplies may be factors in the spread of the disease. Burial rituals that involve close contact with the body of a person who has died from the disease also can result in the spread of Ebola. The surfaces of bodies of deceased victims remain infectious for more than a week. In addition, a small percentage of Ebola-infected individuals may remain asymptomatic; such persons may unknowingly carry and spread the virus. Ebolaviruses have an incubation period of 2 to 21 days. The onset of illness is sudden and harsh. Infected persons may develop fever, severe headaches and muscle aches, and loss of appetite. Within a few days the virus causes a condition known as disseminated intravascular coagulation, which is marked by both blood clots and hemorrhaging. In the case of Ebola, clots are concentrated in the liver, spleen, brain, and other internal organs, forcing capillaries to bleed into surrounding tissue. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea with blood and mucus, conjunctivitis, and sore throat soon follow. A maculopapular rash (discolored elevations of the skin) appears on the trunk and quickly spreads to the limbs and head. The patient is then beset by spontaneous bleeding from body orifices and any breaks in the skin, such as injection sites, and within the gastrointestinal tract, skin, and internal organs. Death is usually brought on by hemorrhaging, shock, or renal failure and occurs within 8 to 17 days. Persons who survive Ebola infection may experience post-Ebola syndrome, symptoms of which include vision problems (potentially blindness), headaches, severe joint and muscle pain, and extreme fatigue. Treatment Treatment for Ebola is primarily with supportive care, including fluids, electrolytes, and medications to stabilize blood pressure and manage complications. Early treatment greatly improves survival. For infections caused by the Zaire strain of Ebola virus, targeted antibody therapies such as REGN-EB3 (Inmazeb) and mAb114 (Ebanga) can help reduce mortality. Other treatments that had been investigated for Ebola included the antiviral drug remdesivir (RDV) and ZMapp, a mixture of three antibodies that bind to proteins on ebolaviruses. ZMapp was administered to infected individuals during the 2014–16 outbreak, though its effectiveness was unclear. In trials during the 2018–20 Ebola outbreak, both REGN-EB3 and mAb114 were found to be more effective at reducing Ebola-related mortality compared with RDV and ZMapp. REGN-EB3 and mAb114 were approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2020. Ebola virus disease; hand washingA Liberian nurse washing his hands with water after treating a patient sick with Ebola virus disease in Monrovia, Liberia, during the 2014–15 outbreak.(more) The spread of ebolaviruses can be contained by barrier nursing, handling of infected blood and tissue in isolated laboratory units, and proper decontamination of reusable equipment. Experimental vaccines are under development for Ebola, including a vaccine known as VSV-EBOV, which was found to be highly effective in preventing the spread of ebolavirus among persons in close contact with infected individuals. VSV-EBOV was a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV)-based vaccine that expressed an EBOV glycoprotein. When VSV-EBOV was injected, the vaccinated individuals generated antibodies against the EBOV protein, thereby gaining immunity. Survivors of Ebola infection may be affected by a constellation of long-term health complications known as post-Ebola syndrome. In follow-up studies of persons who recovered from acute Ebola infection, many were found to suffer from uveitis (eye redness and pain), vision loss, tinnitus, hearing loss, stroke, headaches, muscle and joint pain, and other abnormalities in musculoskeletal and neurological function. Some affected individuals also suffered renal failure and were at increased risk of premature death. Post-Ebola syndrome is treated primarily by symptom management with drugs such as analgesics (pain relievers) and anti-inflammatory agents. Britannica Editors History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Top Questions What are viral hemorrhagic fevers? Viral hemorrhagic fevers are a group of highly dangerous illnesses caused by viruses that damage the vascular system, leading to severe bleeding. Initial symptoms include fever, fatigue, muscle aches, and exhaustion. These viruses belong to four families: Flaviviridae, Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Filoviridae. Specific animals or insects often transmit them, restricting these diseases to certain geographic areas. Examples include dengue, yellow fever, Lassa fever, and Ebola. Transmission to humans usually occurs via contact with infected animals like rodents and insects. Avoiding contact with these hosts and controlling their populations can prevent infection. Isolation of infected individuals can also prevent the virus from spreading from person to person. 2 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. Which viruses can cause viral hemorrhagic fevers? Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) are a group of severe illnesses characterized by bleeding, fever, and shock. These diseases are caused by viruses from four families: Flaviviridae, Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Filoviridae. Flaviviruses Dengue and yellow fever viruses, often transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, are the most common causes. While yellow fever affects the liver and causes severe bleeding, dengue induces only minor bleeding but can result in dengue shock syndrome. Arenaviruses are spread to humans through contact with food or soil contaminated by rodent excreta. This family of viruses causes Lassa fever, Argentine hemorrhagic fever, Bolivian hemorrhagic fever, Brazilian hemorrhagic fever, and Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever. Bunyaviridae includes Hantaviruses, Rift Valley fever virus, and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus. Hantaviruses are transmitted to humans through rodent contact, while Rift Valley fever is a mosquito-borne disease. Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever is a tick-borne disease. Filoviruses such as Ebola virus and Marburg virus, are highly fatal and may also cause disease in primates. The origin of filovirus epidemics remains unclear, but scientists suspect that fruit bats may be responsible for outbreaks of Marburg disease. 2 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. How do viral hemorrhagic fevers affect the human body? Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) are a group of highly dangerous illnesses caused by bloodborne viruses that harm the vascular system, resulting in significant bleeding. Initial symptoms include fever, fatigue, and muscle aches. The viruses attack cells and may suppress the immune system, which allows the virus to reproduce. Disseminated intravascular coagulation, a condition marked by blood clots and hemorrhaging, can occur. Clots concentrated in organs force capillaries to bleed into surrounding tissue. This leads to bleeding from body openings, the gastrointestinal tract, skin, and internal organs. Some VHFs, such as dengue, induce only minor bleeding that is rarely fatal, while others, such as Ebola, can cause death in up to 90% of victims. 4 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever Ebola: Course of infection Marburgvirus bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. What role do blood vessels play in the disease process? In viral hemorrhagic fevers, blood vessels play a central role in the disease process. These diseases are caused by bloodborne viruses that damage the vascular system, leading to extensive bleeding internally, externally, and under the skin. Symptoms often include fever, fatigue, muscle aches, and exhaustion. These viruses are typically transmitted to humans via animals such as rodents and insects. There are no vaccines available, and treatment is mainly supportive. Preventing infection involves avoiding contact with host species and controlling rodent and insect populations. Isolation of infected individuals can also prevent human-to-human spread through physical contact. 2 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. Why do people with these fevers sometimes bleed or bruise easily? Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) are a group of illnesses caused by bloodborne viruses that damage the vascular system. This damage leads to bleeding under the skin, in internal organs, and from body orifices. Several factors contribute to the ease of bleeding and bruising: * Vascular Damage VHFs can cause vascular damage. * Coagulation Abnormalities Viral infections can cause abnormalities in blood clotting. * Cytokine Release Unregulated cytokine production may lead to vascular damage and hemorrhaging. Some VHFs are highly fatal; certain Ebola strains have mortality rates of up to 90%. Isolation of infected individuals helps prevent the spread of VHFs, as transmission can occur through physical contact. 3 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever Marburgvirus bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. How does the body respond to fight off a viral hemorrhagic fever? Viral hemorrhagic fevers are a group of severe illnesses caused by various virus families that damage the vascular system, leading to bleeding. The body's response involves several complex mechanisms. The infection typically begins with the virus entering the body through contact with an infected animal or insect. Once inside, the virus targets cells in the vascular system, such as endothelial cells, which line blood vessels. The damage to these cells leads to increased vascular permeability and impaired blood clotting. This results in both internal and external hemorrhaging, as blood leaks from the vessels. The immune system responds by releasing cytokines, which are signaling molecules that help coordinate the immune response. However, in severe cases, this can lead to a "cytokine storm," where an excessive amount of cytokines are released, causing inflammation, shock, and organ failure. 2 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. Show more Show less viral hemorrhagic fever, any of a variety of highly fatal viral diseases that are characterized by massive external or internal bleeding or bleeding into the skin. Other symptoms vary by the type of viral hemorrhagic fever but often include fever, malaise, muscle aches, vomiting, and shock. Most viral hemorrhagic fevers are geographically restricted because they are transmitted by specific animal or insect hosts (reservoirs) that occupy narrow and sometimes localized ecological niches. Viral hemorrhagic fevers are caused by viruses of four families: Flaviviridae, Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Filoviridae. The most common viral hemorrhagic fevers are dengue and yellow fever, caused by related mosquito-borne flaviviruses, often being transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. In the late 18th century, yellow fever epidemics in American coastal cities caused widespread panic, but the disease currently occurs only in developing countries of Africa and South America. It is the only major viral hemorrhagic fever for which an effective preventive vaccine exists and is widely used. Most cases of dengue, seen in tropical areas, are mild and influenza-like, but all four dengue viruses may produce dengue hemorrhagic fever or its severe form, dengue shock syndrome. Unlike yellow fever, which affects the liver and causes severe bleeding, dengue involves the liver only minimally and tends to induce only minor bleeding that is rarely fatal. However, if dengue shock syndrome occurs, patients may die when fluids and electrolytes in their vascular compartments shift into tissues, collapsing the blood volume and precipitating low blood pressure and shock. Dengue is unique among the fatal hemorrhagic fevers in that even severe cases can be effectively treated with simple fluid administration. The arenaviruses are highly adapted to specific rodent hosts, which may become silently infected and excrete the virus in feces, urine, and saliva. However, when humans come into contact with food or soil contaminated by these rodent excreta, disease may result. The arenaviruses cause the diseases Lassa fever (occurring in Africa), Argentine hemorrhagic fever, Bolivian hemorrhagic fever, Brazilian hemorrhagic fever, and Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever.
